title: Psalm 101: A King's Vow of Integrity
summary: A king promises to sing of God's loving devotion and justice and then vows how he will live and rule. At home he will walk with integrity and keep worthless things from his eyes. At court he will silence slanderers, refuse the proud, choose faithful people as his servants, bar liars from his presence, and every morning remove the wicked from the city of the LORD.
story: After the run of psalms proclaiming that the LORD reigns (Psalms 93 to 100), Book IV turns in Psalm 101 to a human king. The placement matters. The collection has been responding to the collapse of David's dynasty lamented in Psalm 89, and it has done so by pointing to God's own kingship. Now it asks what a king under that King should look like. Psalm 101 answers with a vow that begins in the king's private life and moves outward to his household, his servants, and his city. It stands as both a standard for Israel's kings and, in light of how most of them actually ruled, an indictment of them.
historical:
The heading reads “A Psalm of David”. The Hebrew phrase, ledavid, can mean by David, for David, or belonging to the Davidic collection, and scholars debate how much the headings tell us: some regard them as reliable early tradition about authorship, others as later editorial notes about how psalms were grouped and used. Many readers take this psalm as a king's declaration at his coronation or at a yearly renewal of his duties, a kind of royal oath before God. Some older commentators linked the question “when will You come to me?” (verse 2) to David's fearful question when the ark was being brought to Jerusalem, how the ark of the LORD could come to him (2 Samuel 6:9), but the connection is a suggestion, not something the psalm states.

The king's duty to judge fits the monarchy's practice. Absalom stood by the city gate in the early morning to intercept people bringing cases to David (2 Samuel 15:2), and Jeremiah later commanded the house of David to administer justice every morning (Jeremiah 21:12). A psalm from any period of the monarchy could draw on that expectation, and after the monarchy ended it would have been read as a portrait of the king Israel still hoped for.
cultural:
Ancient Near Eastern kings publicly claimed to be just. Hammurabi of Babylon (eighteenth century BC) opened and closed his law collection by presenting himself as the shepherd who protected the weak, and other rulers made similar boasts in their inscriptions. Psalm 101 shares that ideal but differs in where it starts. Before the king speaks of anyone else's behavior, he speaks of his own heart, his own eyes, and his own house.

A king's court was full of people who wanted access and favor. Slander, flattery, and whispered accusations were the ordinary tools of court politics, as the stories of Saul's and David's courts show. The king's promise to silence those who slander “in secret” (verse 5) and to choose servants from “the faithful of the land” (verse 6) is a promise about the character of government. The morning was the time for hearing cases, and “the city of the LORD” (verse 8) was Jerusalem, God's city before it was the king's.
literary: The psalm is a string of first-person vows, almost all in the form “I will” or “shall not”. After an opening line of praise (verse 1), verses 2 to 4 concern the king himself: his way, his house, his eyes, his heart. Verses 5 to 8 turn to others: whom he will not endure and whom he will welcome. The two halves are linked by repeated words: the way of integrity (verses 2 and 6), eyes (verses 3, 5, and 6), and the house (verses 2 and 7). The single question in verse 2, “when will You come to me?”, interrupts the vows and shows that the king knows he cannot keep them without God's presence. The movement from inner life to public order is the psalm's argument: justice in the city starts with integrity in the house.

outline.t: A song of loving devotion and justice
The king's own heart and house
Whom the king will refuse and whom he will welcome
Every morning, justice in the city of the LORD

doctrines.note: Human authority is accountable to God. The king rules in “the city of the LORD”, and his task is to reflect God's loving devotion and justice, the two qualities the psalm names first.
Integrity begins privately: in what one looks at, what one clings to, and how one lives at home. The psalm refuses to separate public justice from personal holiness.
The king's choice of companions and servants shapes his rule. Keeping the faithful near and the deceitful away is practical wisdom that runs through Proverbs as well.

words.note: Tamim, blameless, whole, complete. Used of sacrificial animals without defect and of people whose lives are undivided, like Noah (Genesis 6:9). It does not mean sinless but wholehearted, a life with no hidden second agenda.

Beliyaal, worthlessness, often translated “worthless” or left as the name Belial. In the Old Testament it describes scoundrels and destructive schemes. The king refuses to set any such thing before his eyes, a vow about what he will allow into his attention.
Boqer, morning. The morning was when kings and judges heard cases (2 Samuel 15:2; Jeremiah 21:12). “Every morning” signals that justice is daily work, not an occasional campaign.

Chesed, loving devotion or covenant loyalty. The psalm opens by singing of God's chesed and justice together, and the rest of the psalm shows a king trying to mirror both: loyalty to the faithful and justice against the wicked.

christ: Israel's history is mostly the story of kings who did not keep this vow, starting with David himself, who looked at what he should not have and took another man's wife (2 Samuel 11). The psalm therefore became part of Israel's hope for a king who would. Christians see that king in Jesus, who is without sin (Hebrews 4:15), who welcomes the humble and resists the proud, and who will one day remove every evildoer from God's city (Revelation 21:27 describes nothing unclean entering the new Jerusalem). The link is a pattern: the psalm draws the portrait, and the Gospels present the one who fits it. At the same time, the psalm's picture of integrity at home and in public still speaks to anyone who holds authority.

hard.q: Isn't a king who silences slanderers and cuts off evildoers every morning describing a harsh or even tyrannical regime?
hard.a: Read today, the language of silencing and cutting off can sound like a ruler crushing dissent. The psalm's context points elsewhere. The people removed are slanderers who ruin their neighbors in secret, the arrogant, liars, and those who practice wickedness, the very people who prey on the weak in a corrupt court. The king's power is exercised in “the city of the LORD” and under the vow of integrity he has first applied to himself. Interpreters differ on whether “cut off” means execution, banishment, or removal from office, and the Hebrew can cover all three. The danger the reader senses is real, since kings who claimed this psalm's ideals often abused them, which is why the Old Testament also records the prophets holding kings to account.

questions: The king starts with his own house and eyes before judging anyone else. Why does the order matter for anyone who holds responsibility?
Verse 3 speaks of setting no worthless thing before one's eyes. What would that look like in a world of screens?
Whom do you keep closest to you, and what does that choice say about the kind of person you are becoming?
